<a id="entry-feat-init-repo-feature-lifecycle-persona-skills-with-enforced-phase-gate"></a>

## Entry 1 — 2026-10-29 — feat(init-repo): feature lifecycle persona skills with enforced phase gates

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

Working straight from idea to code without role changes led to fatigue, skipped thinking and chasing side issues. The team shares persona skills, reviews each other's work, generates every artefact with AI (no hand edits), and uses four agents in order of precedence: Claude, Codex, Kiro, opencode. Handoffs needed to be visible to colleagues, and phase order needed enforcing rather than relying on discipline.

## Decision

Ship the lifecycle as part of the per-repo `init-repo` kit rather than as a marketplace plugin, so every agent sees the same skills. GitHub issues are the status source of truth (a parent feature issue with one sub-issue per phase, or a single checklist issue in lite mode); files under `docs/features/<slug>/` hold content. All gate logic lives in one deterministic script invoked by both skills and CI, using only the `gh` CLI. Pushback reopens an earlier phase; explicit ADRs are allowed; the developer phase stops after the detailed plans; acceptance has a scripted walkthrough and an executable test in both local and deployed environments. CODEOWNERS and the admin merge override are kept as they are. Rejected: per-agent skill variants (drift), MCP-based GitHub access (not available in every agent or in Actions), and an issue-event workflow to re-run checks after pushback (deferred for simplicity).

## Consequences

Phase PRs in target repos must close their phase sub-issue and pass `feature-gate`; a PR closing two phases of one feature is blocked until split, and an unreadable closing reference fails closed (`gate-override` is the escape hatch). Known gaps left open: pushback does not re-run an already-green check, a PR can still edit `feature-gate.yml` itself, a kit update is gated by the old script on the base, `promote` is not idempotent after a partial failure, and lite-mode phase detection relies on branch naming. opencode sees byte-identical duplicate skills from two install paths.

<a id="entry-docs-add-mit-license-and-describe-the-skills-in-the-readme"></a>

## Entry 2 — 2026-10-29 — docs: add MIT license and describe the skills in the README

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The marketplace was private, so installing the plugin needed read access to the repo. It had no
licence, and its README said little about what each skill does. Opening it up needs both a
licence and a README a stranger can read.

## Decision

License the repository under MIT and make it public. The README now lists every skill with its
purpose. Branch protection stays as it is: one code-owner approval, `ai-fingerprint` required,
and `enforce_admins` off so the owner can override. Apache-2.0 was considered and not chosen,
because MIT is shorter and the project has no patent concerns.

## Consequences

Anyone can install, fork and reuse the plugin. The commit history, including author emails, is
now public. The `init-repo` dependency notes still assume local checkouts under
`~/RiderProjects`, with flags to override them.

<a id="entry-feat-lifecycle-slice-dev-plans-into-increments-with-a-stop-at-each-bound"></a>

## Entry 3 — 2026-11-10 — feat(lifecycle): slice dev plans into increments with a stop at each boundary

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The developer phase went straight from the accepted design to one plan and one build. On large features that made the plan PR hard to review, made long detailed plans harder for a small local model to execute, and gave the build no point where it could safely stop while leaving something working. Splitting detailed plans by layer (domain / application / infrastructure / API / web) made this worse, because nothing worked end to end until the last layer was done.

## Decision

Slice every feature by behaviour into increments that can each be deployed on their own, and run the build one increment per session with a stop at each boundary ("pencils down"). Small features are exempt below a threshold of about eight tasks. Rejected alternative: giving each increment its own build phase, PR and gate. That would mean changing the phase model in `feature.mjs` and the sub-issues, so for now the increment boundary is a checkpoint within the single dev-build phase.

## Consequences

Plans get an increment table, and plan reviews also approve the build order. Builds take more sessions, but each one leaves the system working. Increment boundaries are enforced through the skill and the exit criteria, not by the gate script, so that is left open: if it proves too loose, per-increment gating is the follow-up.
